1.tip: A firewall is a wall around the traffic: it decides what comes in and goes out. Antivirus and antimalware look at files, not connections.
1.why: A firewall checks network traffic to and from your computer and blocks connections that aren't allowed. Antivirus and antimalware scan files and programs instead.

2.cue: block for 30 seconds, 2 failed attempts within 10
2.tip: Read it like a sentence: block-for HOW LONG, attempts HOW MANY, within WHAT TIME. 30, 2, 10.
2.why: The command order is login block-for <seconds to block> attempts <number of tries> within <seconds to count>. So 30 seconds of blocking after 2 failures in 10 seconds.

3.tip: AAA: Authentication = who are you, Authorization = what can you do, Accounting = what did you do (like a bank statement).
3.why: Accounting records what a user does, such as when they logged in and which commands they ran. Proving who you are is authentication, and allowed resources is authorization.

4.tip: Recon = scouting. nslookup and fping just look around to map the network before any real attack.
4.why: Tools like nslookup and fping gather information, such as names, addresses and which hosts are alive. Collecting information before an attack is a reconnaissance attack.

5.tip: Trojan horse = a gift that hides soldiers. Malware disguised as something fun, like a game.
5.why: A Trojan horse pretends to be a useful or fun program, such as a game, so you install it yourself. Attaching to other programs is a virus, and spreading on its own is a worm.

6.cue: difference between a virus and a worm
6.tip: A worm crawls on its own. A virus needs a host program and a user to spread it.
6.why: A worm copies itself and spreads across the network without help. A virus attaches to a host file and needs someone to run that file before it can spread.

7.cue: compromise of data between two end points
7.tip: Between two end points = in the middle. Man-in-the-middle.
7.why: In a man-in-the-middle attack, the attacker sits between two devices and can read or change the data passing between them, while both sides think they talk directly.

8.tip: Gathering info = recon, like scouting before a game. DoS breaks things, it doesn't study them.
8.why: Reconnaissance is the information-gathering step: the attacker maps hosts, ports and services to find weak spots. DoS, dictionary and man-in-the-middle are actual attacks.

9.tip: AuthENTication = idENTity. Prove who you are, like showing an ID card.
9.why: Authentication checks your identity, usually with a username and password. Deciding what you may access is authorization, and logging what you did is accounting.

10.cue: legitimate responses to requests from internal hosts
10.tip: Stateful = remembers the state of the conversation. Only replies to what you asked for get in.
10.why: Stateful packet inspection remembers which connections inside hosts started, so it only lets in traffic that answers those requests and drops unexpected incoming packets.

11.tip: Brute force = guessing over and over. login block-for locks the door after too many wrong guesses.
11.why: A brute-force attack tries many passwords quickly. login block-for stops logins for a while after a set number of failures, which slows the attacker down a lot.

12.tip: SSH = Secure SHell: everything is encrypted. Telnet sends even your password in plain text.
12.why: SSH encrypts the login and all the data in the session, so someone capturing the traffic can't read it. Telnet sends everything, including passwords, as plain text.

13.cue: advantage of using SSH over Telnet
13.tip: The S in SSH stands for Secure. It's not faster or easier, just safe.
13.why: SSH protects the session with encryption, so remote access is secure. Telnet also asks for a login, so authentication is not the difference, and SSH is not faster.

14.tip: IPS = Intrusion PREVENTION System. Prevention means it blocks, not just alerts. An IDS only detects.
14.why: An IPS sits in the traffic path, spots attacks as they happen and blocks them right away. An IDS only detects and alerts without stopping the traffic.

15.tip: Firewall, then firewall, then IPS: stacked like layers of an onion.
15.why: Using several security devices at different points means an attacker must get past one layer after another. This defense in depth is called a layered approach.

16.tip: Redundancy = a spare. If one path breaks, another path keeps the network up.
16.why: Redundancy adds backup paths and devices so that if one link or switch fails, traffic still has another way through. That removes any single point of failure.

17.tip: Real-time = live. Live calls and live video can't wait, so they get priority.
17.why: Voice and video are real-time traffic: delay makes calls choppy and video freeze. Instant messages, FTP and SNMP can wait a moment without trouble.

18.cue: protocol analyzer before a network upgrade
keys: document and analyze network traffic requirements
18.tip: Before you upgrade, measure. The analyzer shows what traffic each segment really needs.
18.why: Capturing traffic shows which applications and how much traffic each segment carries. That lets the company plan the upgrade around real needs instead of guesses.

19.tip: U = Unreachable. A router said: I have no route to that place.
19.why: The output shows U characters. A U means a router along the path sent back an ICMP unreachable message because it had no route to the destination.

keys: without specifying a destination IP address
20.tip: Type just ping and press Enter: the extended ping asks you questions, including the source address.
20.why: Typing ping alone in privileged EXEC mode starts the extended ping, which prompts for options like the destination, repeat count and the source address or interface.

21.tip: Latency = delay. Longer ping times = more delay.
21.why: Latency is how long packets take to travel. If ping round trip times go up compared to the baseline, packets are being delayed somewhere on the path.

22.why: In Cisco ping output, ! is a reply, a period means it timed out, and U means a router sent back destination unreachable, often because it had no route.

23.cue: pings to other computers and gateway fail
23.tip: Failed pings only say something is wrong, not what. It could be the cable, the NIC, the IP settings or the gateway.
23.why: Many problems cause the same failed pings: a bad cable, wrong IP settings, a firewall, or a down gateway. These two tests alone can't tell you which one it is.

24.tip: -6 = IPv6, -4 = IPv4. The number is the IP version, not a count.
24.why: On Windows, the -6 option tells tracert to use IPv6 for the trace. The -4 option forces IPv4. It does not change hops, timeouts or probes.

keys: where a packet was lost or delayed
25.tip: tracert TRACEs the ROUTE hop by hop, so you see the hop where things stop or slow down.
25.why: tracert lists each router along the path and its reply time. If replies stop or get slow at a certain hop, you know where the packet was lost or delayed.

26.cue: show cdp neighbors after a failed ping
26.tip: CDP works at Layer 2, without IP. If CDP sees the neighbor, the link itself works.
26.why: CDP runs at Layer 2 and doesn't need IP addresses. If R1 sees R2 in CDP, the cable and link are fine, so the ping problem is likely at Layer 3, such as IP settings.

27.cue: IP address, host name, IOS version of neighbors
27.tip: Neighbors = CDP. Want the IP and IOS too? Add detail.
27.why: show cdp neighbors detail lists each directly connected Cisco device with its name, IP address, platform and IOS version. show version only shows your own device.

28.tip: show version = the device's ID card: IOS, uptime, memory and the config register (like 0x2102).
28.why: show version shows the IOS version, uptime, hardware, memory and the configuration register value, which controls how the router boots. Routes and interface status are elsewhere.

29.cue: log messages on Telnet or SSH sessions
29.tip: Remote session? Turn on the terminal MONITOR to watch logs.
29.why: Log messages go to the console by default. On a Telnet or SSH session you must enter terminal monitor to see them. logging synchronous only stops messages from breaking your typing.

30.cue: send debug messages to the vty lines
30.tip: vty = remote lines. Remote + logs = terminal monitor.
30.why: The vty lines are for remote Telnet or SSH sessions. terminal monitor makes debug and log messages show up in that remote session.

31.cue: identified a network issue, next step
31.tip: Order: identify problem, theory, test theory, plan, fix and verify, document.
31.why: In the structured troubleshooting process, after you identify the problem you form a theory of probable causes. Next you test it, then plan and apply the fix.

32.cue: ping by IP works but not the domain name
32.tip: IP works, name fails = a DNS problem. nslookup asks DNS directly.
32.why: If the IP address works but the name doesn't, the name-to-address lookup is failing. nslookup queries the DNS server so you can see if names are being resolved.

33.tip: 169.254 = I asked DHCP and nobody answered, so I made up my own address.
33.why: A 169.254.x.x address is APIPA. Windows gives itself one when it is set to get an address automatically but can't reach a DHCP server.

34.cue: prove communication to H1 from the R2 interface
34.tip: Extended ping lets you pick the SOURCE interface, so R2 can ping as if it were H3's gateway.
34.why: A normal ping from R2 uses the outgoing interface as the source. An extended ping lets you set the source to the LAN interface H3 uses, proving that path works.

35.tip: Compare to the baseline: about 100 ms became over 2000 ms. Pings still work, so it's delay, not a broken link.
35.why: The pings still succeed, but the times are many times higher than the baseline. That means packets are being slowed down somewhere between the two networks.

36.tip: DHCP hands out addresses. DNS turns names into addresses.
36.why: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) gives devices an IP address, mask, gateway and DNS server automatically when they join the network.

37.tip: Want to know the way? Look at the route table: show ip route.
37.why: The routing table lists each known network and the exit interface or next hop used to reach it. show ip route displays that table.

38.tip: exec-timeout logs out idle people. People log in on the console and vty lines, not on Ethernet or serial ports.
38.why: exec-timeout ends an idle management session so nobody can use a session someone walked away from. Admins log in through the console and vty lines, so that's where it applies.

39.cue: SSH configuration, login local and transport input ssh
39.tip: SSH needs NKU: a Name (domain), Keys (RSA), and Users (local database).
39.why: The RSA key needs a hostname and domain name, the keys make the encryption, and login local needs a local user database. SSH turns on by itself once the keys exist.

40.tip: Worms exploit holes. Patch the holes and the worm can't get in.
40.why: Worms spread by using security holes in software. Installing the vendor's security updates closes those holes, so the worm can no longer infect the systems.

41.tip: ping = is it there? tracert = how do I get there, hop by hop?
41.why: ping only tells you whether the destination replied and how fast. tracert lists every router along the way, so you see each hop to the destination.

42.tip: Securely + remote device access = SSH. Telnet, FTP and HTTP send plain text.
42.why: SSH gives encrypted remote access to the device's command line, even across off-site links. Telnet and HTTP send logins in plain text, and FTP is for file transfer.

43.tip: transport input ssh = only SSH can come in on the vty lines. Telnet gets turned away.
43.why: In the activity, the vty lines need transport input ssh so remote logins only work through SSH. Without it, Telnet would still be allowed and logins would travel in plain text.

44.tip: A phrase made of several words is long and easy to remember, but hard to guess.
44.why: WhatAreyouwaiting4 is a passphrase: a long string of words with mixed case and a number. Length makes it hard to crack, even though it's easy for you to remember.

keys: minimum of 10 numbers, letters and special characters
45.tip: Count and mix: 10 characters with letters, numbers and symbols = strong.
45.why: pR3s!d7n&0 has 10 characters and mixes upper and lower case letters, numbers and special characters, which makes it very hard to guess or crack.

46.tip: No letters here, just numbers and symbols. So pick the choice that says numbers and special characters only.
46.why: 5$7*4#033! is 10 characters long and mixes numbers with special characters, which makes it strong. It has no letters, so the choice that mentions letters doesn't fit.

48.tip: 1-2-3-4 counting is the first thing attackers try.
48.why: 12345678! is just a counting series with one symbol at the end. Password-cracking tools try simple sequences like this first, so it is weak.

49.tip: admin is what devices ship with, so attackers try it first.
49.why: admin is a common factory default password on new devices. Attackers know default passwords and try them first, so it is weak.

50.tip: A date like Feb121978 looks like a birthday: personal info someone can find.
50.why: Feb121978 looks like a birth date. Personal details like birthdays are easy to find online or guess, so the password is weak.

51.tip: password is at the top of every list of most used passwords.
51.why: password is one of the most common passwords in the world. Attackers always try it early, so the best answer is that it's a commonly used password.

52.tip: A name is personal info, even with mixed capitals. Short too.
52.why: RobErT is a person's name, which an attacker can learn from social media or a staff list. Mixing upper and lower case doesn't make a short name strong.

53.tip: Names = personal info. Names of you, family or pets are easy to find.
53.why: Elizabeth is a person's name, the kind of personal detail an attacker can find and guess. That makes it a weak password.

54.cue: verify the IP addresses of all interfaces
54.tip: All interfaces, one short table: show ip interface brief.
54.why: show ip interface brief lists every router interface on one line each, with its IP address and whether it is up or down.

55.tip: Duplex, speed and errors live in show interfaces.
55.why: show interfaces shows each port's duplex and speed settings, plus error counters like collisions. A duplex mismatch shows up there.

56.tip: On a Windows PC, ipconfig shows its IP setup. show commands are for Cisco devices.
56.why: ipconfig on a Windows PC shows its IP address, subnet mask and default gateway. The show and copy commands only work on Cisco routers and switches.

57.cue: save a router configuration to NVRAM
57.tip: Running (RAM, now) goes to startup (NVRAM, kept after reboot).
57.why: The running config lives in RAM and is lost on reboot. Copying it to the startup config saves it in NVRAM so it loads the next time the router starts.

58.tip: On a Mac, getifaddr = get interface address. en0 is usually Wi-Fi.
58.why: On macOS, ipconfig getifaddr en0 prints the IP address of interface en0, which is usually the wireless interface on Mac laptops.

59.cue: IPv6 interface addresses on a router
59.tip: Need IPv6? Put ipv6 in the command: show ipv6 interface.
59.why: show ipv6 interface displays the IPv6 addresses on the router's interfaces, including link-local and global addresses. The other commands are IPv4 or not about addresses.

60.tip: PC problem = PC command. ipconfig shows the default gateway.
60.why: ipconfig on the PC shows its IP address, mask and default gateway, so the teacher can check the gateway right on the computer.

61.cue: verify that IPv6 routing has been enabled
61.tip: IPv6 routing is a config line (ipv6 unicast-routing). Find config lines in show running-config.
61.why: IPv6 routing is turned on with ipv6 unicast-routing. To check it's there, you look at the current config with show running-config.

62.cue: determine the IP address of a website
62.tip: nslookup = name server lookup. Give it a name, get the IP back.
62.why: nslookup asks a DNS server for the IP address of a domain name, so you can see the address a website resolves to.

64.cue: Match each weakness with an example
64.tip: Policy = didn't plan. Configuration = set it up wrong (ACL). Technological = flaw in the system itself (OS).
64.why: Not thinking through unauthorized access is a planning (policy) gap. Missing traffic in an ACL is a setup (configuration) mistake. OS flaws are built into the tech (technological).

65.cue: Match the type of information security threat
65.tip: Info theft = steal secrets. Identity theft = pretend to be someone. Data loss = destroy data. Disruption = flood it so nobody gets in.
65.why: Taking secret documents is information theft, using someone's details is identity theft, destroying recordings is data loss, and flooding a site with requests disrupts service.

66.cue: Match the description to the type of firewall filtering
66.tip: Packet = addresses. Application = ports. URL = web addresses. Stateful = only replies to what you asked for.
66.why: Packet filtering checks IP or MAC addresses, application filtering checks port numbers, URL filtering checks web addresses or keywords, and stateful inspection allows replies to inside requests.

67.cue: steps needed to configure a switch for SSH
67.tip: SSH needs: domain name, RSA keys, local user, login local, transport input ssh. Not login or password cisco.
67.why: SSH needs a domain name for the keys, RSA keys for encryption, a local user, login local so the lines use it, and transport input ssh. login and password cisco are for plain line passwords.
